passage: Leap years. That's where it went wrong. I'm Trisha, I'm twenty-two, and my hardest moment in my first month as team lead was about a date parser. Deepika, our newest developer, had written her own: eight hundred lines, three weekends. It mostly worked. But the standard library already does the same job, tested by thousands of people, and her version kept breaking on leap years. In the review I suggested we switch. She went pale and said, "But I built it from scratch." Not "it works better." Just that she built it. I get it. In college I kept a clumsy app of mine alive for a whole year for the same reason. So we agreed to run both versions on the test data for a week and let the results speak.

qa.q: What did Deepika's version keep breaking on?
qa.a: It kept breaking on leap years.

qa.q: What does Deepika's reply "But I built it from scratch" show about why she wants to keep her parser?
qa.a: She feels proud of the parser for the three weekends she put into it, not for how well it works, so replacing it feels like losing her own work.

qa.q: Which choice did Trisha make, and why might it help?
qa.a: Trisha suggested running both versions on the test data for a week, which lets the evidence decide without dismissing Deepika's effort in a single meeting.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel when the team lead suggests switching in the review?
qa.a: She may feel her three weekends are being thrown away in front of others, which is why she goes pale and defends the effort instead of the results. 😔

grounding: A young team lead notices a developer clinging to her own hand-written code because of the effort spent, even though a standard library would serve better.

passage: Minakshi here, lead for our college hackathon team. Writing this in the team notes so I remember it. Sharmila spent two nights writing her own login system for our app. When the mentor said the open-source library handles passwords more safely and would save us hours, Sharmila kept scrolling through her code, saying, "But look how neat the functions are." She didn't argue about safety at all. She talked about how late she had stayed up. I can't know what she was feeling, but she hugged her laptop when the mentor left. We're twenty hours from the deadline. I think the library is the better tool. I also think I should thank her for those two nights before I ask her to let it go.

qa.q: How many nights did Sharmila spend writing her own login system?
qa.a: Two nights.

qa.q: What do Sharmila's comments about neat functions and staying up late suggest?
qa.a: She seems attached to her login system because of the effort she poured into it, rather than because it is safer or better than the library.

qa.q: What does Minakshi plan to do before asking Sharmila to switch, and why is that wise?
qa.a: Minakshi plans to thank her for the two nights first, so the switch is about the better tool and does not feel like a rejection of her effort. 🙏

qa.q: What might the mentor be focused on that Sharmila is not?
qa.a: The mentor is thinking about safer password handling and saving hours before the deadline, while Sharmila is thinking about her own late nights.

grounding: A student team lead notices a teammate valuing her self-written login code for the effort it took, not for how well it serves the project.

passage:
Day one: Vandana, twenty-two and newly made team lead at a Kochi billing office, watched intern Madhuri proudly demo a script she had written to sort invoices. It took forty seconds per file.
Day four: Vandana showed her the office's standard reporting tool, which did the same job in two seconds and handled rupee symbols correctly. Madhuri nodded, then quietly kept using her script. "I've already fixed so many bugs in it," she said, eyes on her screen.
Day nine: A client complained about a mis-sorted invoice. It came from the script. Madhuri looked stricken. Vandana pulled up a chair beside her. "Your script taught you a lot. Let's keep a copy, and use the tool for clients." Madhuri let out a long breath and opened the tool.

qa.q: How long did Madhuri's script take per file?
qa.a: Forty seconds per file.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri keep using her script after seeing the faster tool?
qa.a: She felt tied to it because she had already fixed so many bugs in it, and all that effort made it feel worth more than the job it did.

qa.q: Which choice on day nine helped Madhuri let go of the script?
qa.a: Vandana sat beside her, said the script taught her a lot and suggested keeping a copy while using the tool for clients. That honoured the effort without keeping the flawed tool.

qa.q: How is the client affected by Madhuri's attachment to the script?
qa.a: The client got a mis-sorted invoice, so the attachment stopped being a private matter and caused a real problem for someone outside the team.

grounding: A new team lead watches an intern cling to her own slow script for the effort spent, until a client problem shows it serves the work badly.

passage: Uma, you asked old Jaya from the third floor how to handle Kiran and his home-made login code. Well. When I was twenty-two, I led my first team, three of us, at a small Chennai startup. Our quietest developer, Ravi, had written his own sorting routine for the billing system. Three weekends of work. The standard library already had one that was faster and tested by thousands of people. I suggested we switch. Ravi went pale. He didn't argue about speed. He talked about the weekends, and the clever part he'd figured out on a bus. That's when I noticed: he loved it for what it cost him, not for what it did. I didn't win by arguing. I asked him to run both on a big file and time them. His took four minutes, the library's took six seconds. He was quiet for a while. Then he said, 'Okay. But can I keep mine?' Of course, I said.

qa.q: How long did Ravi's sorting routine take on the big file?
qa.a: His took four minutes, while the library's took six seconds.

qa.q: What did Jaya realise when Ravi talked about his weekends?
qa.a: Jaya realised Ravi loved the routine for what it cost him, not for what it did, since he never argued about speed.

qa.q: What could Uma try with Kiran, based on this story?
qa.a: Uma could ask Kiran to compare his login code with the standard library on a real test, rather than arguing, and let him keep his version.

qa.q: How might Ravi have felt when the timings came in?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and quiet at first, but asking to keep his version shows he could accept the result while still valuing his work.

grounding: A senior engineer tells a young lead how, at twenty-two, they noticed a developer clinging to a hand-written routine because of the effort spent, not how well it worked.

passage: The college fest's ticket website was due to open at six in the evening, and at noon it was crashing every few minutes. Indu, twenty-one and leading the student tech team, traced it to one place: Vaibhav's hand-written image uploader. He had spent two weeks on it. The standard library the rest of the site used could do the same job in ten lines. 'Let's swap it,' Indu said. Vaibhav didn't look up from his screen. 'I just need to fix one thing.' At two, he said the same. At three, he showed her how clever his resizing trick was, the one he'd worked out at midnight. Indu noticed he never said the uploader was better. Only that he'd built it. At four she said, 'We'll keep your code in a folder. Let's use the library for tonight.' He nodded slowly and closed the file.

qa.q: When was the ticket website due to open?
qa.a: It was due to open at six in the evening.

qa.q: What did Indu realise from how Vaibhav talked about his uploader?
qa.a: She realised he never said it was better, only that he'd built it, which suggested he valued it for the effort he'd spent.

qa.q: Which choice by Indu helped at four o'clock, and why?
qa.a: Keeping his code in a folder while using the library honoured Vaibhav's effort but let the site work for the deadline.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have felt closing the file?
qa.a: He probably felt disappointed and a bit sore after two weeks and a midnight trick, but may also have been relieved his work wasn't just thrown away.

grounding: A student team lead notices a developer clinging to his hand-written uploader because of the effort spent, even though a standard library would serve better.
